  • cfbfastR 114 17
    An R package to quickly obtain clean and tidy college football play by play data
  • hoopR 158 28
    An R package to quickly obtain clean and tidy men's basketball play by play data.
  • wehoop 52 7
    An R package to quickly obtain clean and tidy women's basketball play by play data.
  • sportsdataverse-js 89 19
    Retrieves sports data from a popular sports website as well as from the NCAA website, with support for NBA, WNBA, NFL, NHL, College Football and mens and womens college basketball,
  • sportsdataverse-py 133 22
    Tidy sports data in Python: play-by-play, box scores, schedules, rosters and models across 100+ leagues (NFL, NBA, WNBA, MLB, NHL, college sports, soccer, international basketball and hockey). polars-first.

Hi, I'm Saiem 👋


I'm a machine learning engineer, computer vision by trade, and the creator and maintainer of the SportsDataverse: R, Python and JavaScript packages that make public sports data easy to get at. They share the same ideas about tidy data, the same automated release pipeline and, where it matters, the same models. I have spent most of my evenings since 2020 on it, and the goal hasn't changed: take the gathering out of the way of the research.

What I'm working on now

  • The R packages finished a long CRAN campaign in 2026. cfbfastR, hoopR, wehoop, fastRhockey, baseballr, oddsapiR and cfbseedR are all current on CRAN; the rest of the family installs from sportsdataverse.r-universe.dev.
  • sportsdataverse-py was rebuilt end to end on polars. ESPN across every league, the NBA and WNBA stats APIs, NHL, MLB and Statcast, HockeyTech, stats.ncaa.org, plus the same loaders and models the R packages ship.
  • Models ship with the data. Every load_*() function reads automated releases (sportsdataverse-data): play-by-play, box scores, schedules, rosters and, increasingly, fitted models (expected points, win probability, shot quality, expected goals) with the training code committed beside them.
  • Public data status. sportsdataverse.org/status shows, nightly, how fresh every producer's data is and whether its pipeline is passing.
  • Logos, colors and headshots for plots and tables: sdvplotR for ggplot2, gt and reactable, its Python sibling sdvplot on PyPI, and the TypeScript port sdvplot-js on npm, which adds sportyR's playing surfaces.
  • Blazing the Nets, rebuilt. My 2021 Brooklyn Nets shooting dashboard, now on d3 v7 and Next.js and reading release parquet files at request time (write-up).
  • The lab on my site: small, runnable ideas, like querying a release file from the browser with DuckDB.

Latest notes

From saiemgilani.com/notes, refreshed daily from the site's RSS feed.

  • Blazing the Nets, rebuilt on d3 v7
  • The badge that lies
  • cfbseedR: Simulate and Evaluate College Football Seasons
  • sportsdataversedata: sportsdataverse data storage functions
  • sdvplotR: Sports Team Logo Plots in 'ggplot2', 'gt' and 'reactable'

Packages I build and maintain

Package What it covers Version Downloads
cfbfastR (source) College football play-by-play, EPA and win probability
hoopR (source) Men's basketball: ESPN, the NBA Stats API, KenPom, stats.ncaa.org
wehoop (source) Women's basketball: ESPN, the WNBA Stats API, stats.ncaa.org
fastRhockey (source) NHL, PWHL and the HockeyTech leagues
baseballr (source) Bill Petti's baseball package, which I maintain
oddsapiR (source) Sports odds from The Odds API
cfbseedR (source) College football season simulation and playoff seeding
cfb4th (source) Fourth-down decisions
cfbplotR (source) College football logos and colors for ggplot2
sdvplotR (source) Logos, colors, headshots and themes across leagues for ggplot2, gt and reactable
recruitR (source) College recruiting rankings
usfootballR (source) MLS and NWSL from ESPN
sportsdataverse (R) (source) The meta-package that installs and loads the family
sportsdataverse (Python) (source) Every league above in one polars-first package
sdvplot (source) Python sibling of sdvplotR
sdvplot-js (source) TypeScript port of sdvplot/sdvplotR and sportyR: team identity, colors, logos, playing surfaces, tables
sportsdataverse (Node.js) (source) ESPN, 247Sports and NCAA endpoints for Node.js

Every package has a printable one-page cheat sheet at sportsdataverse.org/cheatsheets.

Data status

Live, from the nightly ecosystem snapshot. Out of season a league reads idle rather than stale; red means its update pipeline failed.

Projects

Game on Paper

Live college football analytics built on the same expected-points and win-probability models the packages ship (source).

More

  • Blazing the Nets: Brooklyn Nets shot charts, hex maps and shooting signatures (source).
  • saiemgilani.com: notes on each package, written one at a time, and the lab.
  • Sports-Research-Papers: a curated reading list of sports analytics research.

Talks and writing

I presented the SportsDataverse at the Carnegie Mellon Sports Analytics Conference in 2021. The paper won the Data and Software contribution in the reproducible research competition's open track. Slides · Repository · Paper

The notes on my site pick up where that paper left off, one package at a time.

Projects I contribute to

  • ncaascrapR: Eric Hess's NCAA scraper (source)
  • The FSU Sports Analytics Club course packages, fsu-sac and fsu-sac-2025
  • Community packages in the SportsDataverse family: sportyR / sportypy, softballR, mlbplotR and more SportsDataverse packages

GitHub activity

Languages and tools

Data and ML: Python, R, polars, pandas, DuckDB, XGBoost, scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, OpenCV

Web and apps: TypeScript, React, Next.js, Node.js, d3, FastAPI

Infrastructure: Docker, GitHub Actions, Vercel, AWS, GCP, Azure, Linux

Support

If the packages save you time, you can help keep the data flowing: · release notes and new datasets by email at sportsdataverse.org/join.

Earlier work
  • cfbscrapR (archived): the college football scraper that became cfbfastR
  • cfbfastR-py, hoopR-py and wehoop-py (archived): folded into sportsdataverse-py
  • sportsdataverse-nhl: an NHL API TypeScript module

Projects   ·   About   ·   Toolbox   ·   Activity


✦ Featured Projects

PI-Desktop

Your AI Agents. Your Desktop. Your Way.

A local-first desktop workspace for AI coding agents.

Bring your own models, work with persistent sessions, extend the desktop with plugins and tools, and keep your development workflow under your control.


◈ Multi-model ◈ Local-first
◈ Plugin System ◈ Agent Tools
◈ Remote Dev ◈ Persistent Sessions

TypeScript · React · Electron · Rust · SQLite


Explore Project →   ·   Releases →

▸ Why PI-Desktop?

PI-Desktop explores what happens when AI coding agents become a real desktop workspace instead of another temporary chat interface.

The focus is not only the agent itself, but everything around it:

  • models
  • projects
  • sessions
  • plugins
  • tools
  • remote environments
  • persistent state

The goal is to turn AI agents into software you can actually live in every day.

FileCodeBox

Share files and text like picking up a package.

A lightweight self-hosted file and text sharing service.

Upload something, get a passcode, and let another person retrieve it — no account, no complicated workflow.


◈ Self-hosted ◈ Lightweight
◈ Passcode Share ◈ No Account
◈ Docker Ready ◈ Simple API

Python · FastAPI · Vue 3 · SQLite · Docker


Explore Project →   ·   Documentation →

▸ Why FileCodeBox?

The idea is intentionally simple:

Upload something. Get a code. Send the code.

The other person enters it and retrieves the content.

No account creation. No cloud-drive setup. No unnecessary workflow.

Just a small tool that solves one problem well.

◇ About

I like turning recurring problems into small, focused products.

Local-first

Keep data and workflows under the user's control.

Useful first

Solve the real problem before adding complexity.

Extensible

Give users and developers room to make tools their own.

Long-term

Shipping is the start. Reliability and iteration come next.
▸ How I like to build software

I prefer software that feels simple on the surface but leaves enough depth underneath.

That usually means:

  • sensible defaults
  • fewer unnecessary abstractions
  • local ownership of data
  • transparent behavior
  • extensibility where it matters
  • continuous iteration after release

Most of my work sits somewhere between developer tools, AI agents, desktop software, self-hosting, and automation.

Harsh Dayal · Kaos599
AI Engineer · building multi-agent systems, RAG pipelines, and LLM evals at Spectatr AI
LangGraph · MCP · vector memory · LangSmith observability
Google GenAI Exchange Hackathon Winner












// The Build Philosophy

The tools I can't stop thinking about share one property: they make you feel something before they explain themselves. The interface communicates intent. The system has a point of view. The experience is inseparable from the function.

Most software solves the problem and calls it done. I want the version that also makes you go oh, this was built by someone who cares about me as a user.

That means different things depending on what I'm building:

If it's an agent system It shouldn't just work; it should be legible. You should be able to watch it think. State transitions, memory writes, tool calls. LangGraph makes the architecture the product.
If it's an ML model The loss curve is aesthetic. Watching a model learn to separate signal from noise is one of the most satisfying things I know. I care about what the architecture is doing at every layer, not just the final metric.
If it's an interface The terminal is enough canvas. Dense information, monospace type, a palette that doesn't apologize. If it looks like a cockpit, it probably works like one.
If it's a backend It should be invisible in the right way. No drama, no surprises, fast enough that the frontend never has to apologize for it. MCP protocol, FastAPI. Tools that stay out of the way.

The constraint I keep coming back to: a beautiful thing that doesn't solve the problem is art. A solution that's ugly is a missed opportunity. I want both, every time.

∞ The Eternal Curiosity Problem

I have a condition. It starts with one question: why does attention scale like this? Three hours later I'm reading a 1976 paper on Byzantine fault tolerance wondering if distributed consensus has anything useful to say about multi-agent routing. (It does.)

Some rabbit holes I've genuinely gone down: why transformers work when the theoretical guarantees are so weak · whether human memory consolidation during sleep maps to agent memory architectures · what makes a color palette actually good · the geometry of high-dimensional vector spaces and why cosine similarity is weirder than it looks.

"The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in mind at the same time and still retain the ability to function." - F. Scott Fitzgerald, unknowingly describing debugging at 2am.
